root.note: aḍ-ḍayʕa. The Arabic word also meant a farm or country estate.

history: Aldeia, ‘village’, is Arabic: aḍ-ḍayʕa, ‘the village’, a word that could also mean a country estate. The al- at the start is the Arabic article again, as in almofada, a word for ‘the’ fused into the Portuguese noun. In Portugal the word is full of feeling. A aldeia is where many families come from: the grandparents' house in the interior, the August holidays, the village festa with music in the square. Cities fill up in the week and empty towards the aldeias in summer. Portugal also has aldeias históricas, a network of restored historic villages in the centre of the country. Spanish has the same word, aldea, with one vowel less.
historyEinfach: Aldeia means ‘village’. The word comes from Arabic aḍ-ḍayʕa, ‘the village’. Many Portuguese families have an aldeia in the country. They go there in summer for holidays and village parties. Spanish says aldea.

elsewhere.text: Spanish took the same Arabic word for a village.
In parts of the Arab world, ḍayʕa is still used for a village or a country estate.
